title: Atomisation for a Whole Year: Here is What Happened
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele recounts a year-long classroom inquiry into atomisation, the practice of breaking a complex skill down into its smallest constituent concepts and teaching each in isolation before chaining them together. Working with a low-attaining Year 10 maths cohort paralysed by fixed mindsets and blank-page avoidance, he mapped multi-step procedures like solving simultaneous equations into their component sub-skills and drilled each atom separately. The approach eliminated non-attempts and reduced extraneous cognitive load, but introduced new problems of its own, including over-fragmented lessons that lost sight of the whole and the time cost of building atomised resources from scratch. He closes with a practical three-step method for atomising a unit and a caution that the technique should be reserved for lower-attaining sets or genuinely novel content rather than applied universally.
points: Atomisation differs from ordinary 'small steps' by isolating every implicit sub-skill (e.g. the eight distinct atoms inside solving simultaneous equations by elimination) rather than just chunking a mechanical process.
Eliminating 'Blank Page Syndrome' came from students realising they didn't need certainty about the whole route to an answer before starting the first atom.
Over-fragmentation ('Atom Sickness') was fixed by always closing lessons with a full multi-step chained question so students could see how far they'd come.
AI-generated resources were the practical fix for the time cost of atomising every topic, and the resulting materials proved reusable across different classes.
The expertise reversal effect means atomisation should stay targeted at lower-attaining sets or brand-new complex concepts, not applied to students who are already proficient.
quotes: In practice, atomisation requires mapping out every single sub-skill. For example, solving linear simultaneous equations by elimination isn’t just “one skill”, it relies on a chain of 8 distinct sub-atoms

Before this intervention, non-attempts were the biggest drain on student grades. If students didn’t have 100% certainty of the entire route to an answer, they wrote nothing. By isolating individual atoms, students realised they didn’t need to know how to finish the question to start it.
The “Atom Sickness” (Over-Fragmentation): Early on, I spent so much time on isolated atoms that lessons felt fractured. Students lost sight of the overall objective.
Resource Exhaustion: Creating custom, atomised sequences for every single topic is incredibly time-consuming. The Fix: Use of AI generated resources can speed up this process enourmously
Atomisation isn’t about making work “easier” by fragmenting it, it’s about removing unnecessary cognitive noise so students can focus on mastering the underlying mathematical structure.
